passages.t: Why waiting feels longer than it is
passages.q: Why does the same wait feel longer in some places than others?
p: Most people overestimate how long they have waited in a queue. Researchers who study waiting find that the clock is only part of the story. How a wait feels depends heavily on what happens during it, and on what the person waiting knows.

Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time. This is why lifts often have mirrors and why theme parks put screens and games along their queues. When attention has something to hold, fewer minutes seem to pass. Uncertain waits also feel longer than known ones, which is why a sign saying “20 minutes from here” calms a crowd.

The lesson for any business is that shortening a queue is expensive, but changing how the queue feels is often cheap. An airline that moved its baggage hall further from the gates made passengers walk longer but wait less at the carousel, and complaints reportedly fell. The total time barely changed; the empty, idle part did.
g: Waiting time is judged by experience, not just the clock, because what happens during the wait shapes how long it feels.
Idle and uncertain waits feel longest, so giving people something to do or a clear estimate makes waits feel shorter.
Businesses can improve waits cheaply by changing how they feel, because perceived time matters more than actual time.
k: People usually overestimate how long they waited.
Idle and uncertain waits feel longer than occupied and known ones.
Changing how a wait feels is often cheaper than shortening it.

mc.s: What is the main point of the passage?
o: How long a wait feels depends on what happens during it, not just its length
Queues should always be made shorter, whatever the cost
People are bad at telling the time
Airports have the worst queues of any business
mc.e: Every paragraph builds the idea that perceived waiting time is shaped by the experience of the wait.

mc.s: A hospital wants patients to feel less frustrated in its waiting room. Based on the passage, what would help most cheaply?
mc.e: Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones, and a time estimate is cheap compared with extra staff.

mc.s: Why does the author mention the airline’s baggage hall?
o: As an example of changing the feel of a wait rather than its length
To criticise airlines for long walks
To prove that queues are getting shorter
To show that passengers prefer walking to flying
mc.e: The baggage hall story is the concrete case behind the final paragraph’s lesson: same total time, less idle waiting.

o: judge something to be larger than it really is
v.d: To overestimate is to think something is bigger, longer or more than it actually is.
Idle time is time when nothing is happening and you are not doing anything.

passages.q: How did a simple metal box make world trade cheaper?
p: Before the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was slow, skilled work. Dockworkers carried sacks, barrels and crates on board one by one, and a ship could spend more time in port than at sea. Breakages and theft were common, and the cost of handling goods often outweighed the cost of carrying them across the ocean.

In 1956 the American trucking businessman Malcolm McLean sent a ship carrying fifty-eight metal containers from New Jersey to Texas. The idea was simple: pack goods into standard boxes once, at the factory, and move the whole box from truck to ship to train without unpacking. Cranes could lift a container in minutes.

Standard sizes were the real breakthrough. Once ports, ships and lorries around the world agreed on the same dimensions, a box could travel anywhere with almost no handling. Shipping costs fell dramatically, which made it practical to build products in one country from parts made in several others. Much of today’s global supply chain rests on that unglamorous box.
g: Old-style cargo handling was slow, costly and risky because every item was loaded by hand.
McLean’s container idea saved time because goods were packed once and moved as a single box between transport types.
Agreeing on standard sizes made containers transformative because boxes could then move worldwide cheaply, enabling global supply chains.
k: Before containers, handling goods in port was slow, costly and risky.
Containers let goods be packed once and moved between trucks, ships and trains.
Standard sizes cut shipping costs and made global supply chains practical.

mc.s: What does the passage mainly explain?
o: How standardised containers cut the cost of moving goods
Why dockworkers went on strike in the 1950s
Why New Jersey became a major port
mc.e: The passage moves from the old problem to the container and then to standardisation as the reason costs fell.

mc.s: Why would standard sizes matter more than the box itself?
o: A box only saves handling if every port, ship and lorry can take it
Standard boxes are cheaper to paint
Larger boxes always hold more goods
Customers prefer goods in matching boxes
mc.e: The benefit comes from moving the box anywhere without unpacking, which requires everyone to fit the same size.

mc.s: According to the passage, what often cost more than carrying goods across the ocean?
mc.e: The first paragraph says handling costs often outweighed the cost of the sea journey.

v.d: If one thing outweighs another, it is larger or more important than it.
Unglamorous means ordinary or dull rather than attractive or impressive.

passages.q: How do honeybees tell each other where to find food?
p: A honeybee that finds a good patch of flowers does not keep it secret. Back at the hive, she performs a movement that biologists call the waggle dance. Other bees crowd around her in the dark, sensing her movements, and many of them then fly straight to the flowers she found.

The dance works like a map. The bee runs in a straight line while waggling her body, then loops back and repeats. The angle of that straight run, compared with straight up on the honeycomb, matches the angle between the sun and the food. The longer the waggle run lasts, the farther away the food is.

The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch decoded the dance in the mid-twentieth century and shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 partly for this work. His findings showed that animals without large brains can share abstract information. The bees are, in effect, translating a direction relative to the sun into a direction relative to gravity.
g: Bees share food locations with a dance because other bees can then fly directly to good flowers.
The dance encodes direction and distance because the angle of the run shows direction and its length shows distance.
Von Frisch’s decoding mattered because it showed small-brained animals can communicate abstract information.
k: Bees use the waggle dance to direct other bees to food.
The angle of the run gives direction relative to the sun; its length gives distance.
Karl von Frisch decoded it, showing animals can share abstract information.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How the waggle dance tells bees where food is
How flowers attract bees with colour
mc.e: The passage introduces the dance, explains how it encodes location, then notes its scientific importance.

mc.s: A bee dances with a very long waggle run pointing straight up the comb. What does it suggest?
o: Food is far away, in the direction of the sun
Food is very close, away from the sun
mc.e: A long run means far away, and straight up corresponds to the direction of the sun.

mc.s: What does the length of the waggle run communicate?
mc.e: The second paragraph says a longer run means the food is farther away.

v.d: To decode something is to work out what a message or signal means.

o: not physical, existing as an idea
v.d: Abstract information is about ideas or relations, such as a direction, rather than physical objects.

passages.q: Why do some products become more valuable as more people use them?
p: A telephone is useless if you own the only one. It becomes useful when your friends have one, and more useful still when everyone does. Economists call this a network effect: each new user adds value for the existing users, not just for themselves.

Network effects explain why some markets end up dominated by one or two firms. A messaging app with most of your contacts is far more valuable to you than a technically better app with none of them. So users flock to the biggest network, which makes it bigger still. Early leads can turn into lasting advantages.

But network effects are not a guarantee. They can weaken if users can easily belong to several networks at once, as many people do with ride-hailing apps. They can also fail if the network fills with low-quality participants. A large network of spam is worth less than a small network of people you trust. Size matters most when it brings relevant connections.
g: A network effect means each new user makes the product more valuable for everyone because value comes from connections.
Network effects lead to dominance because users join the biggest network, which then grows further.
Network effects can still fail because people can use several networks or the network can fill with low-quality users.
k: In a network effect, each new user adds value for existing users.
This can make the biggest network grow bigger and dominate a market.
The effect weakens when users can join several networks or quality drops.

mc.s: Which sentence best captures the passage?
o: Network effects can create dominant products, but only when the connections stay valuable
The best technology always wins in the end
Telephones were the first network product
Ride-hailing apps have the strongest network effects
mc.e: The passage defines network effects, shows how they create dominance, then gives the limits.

mc.s: Why might a new messaging app struggle even if it is better designed?
o: Users’ contacts are already on the existing app
mc.e: The value of a messaging app comes from who else is on it, so a better design alone does not pull users across.

mc.s: What job does the third paragraph do?
o: It adds limits and exceptions to the idea
It gives the history of the telephone
It repeats the definition in new words
It argues network effects do not exist
mc.e: It begins with “But” and lists conditions under which network effects weaken.

o: controlled by being far stronger than others
v.d: A market dominated by a firm is one where that firm has far more power or share than rivals.

o: a certainty that something will happen
v.d: A guarantee is a promise or certainty. Saying network effects are “not a guarantee” means success is not certain.

passages.q: Why does sleep matter for remembering what you learned?
p: Sleep is not simply the brain switching off. During sleep the brain is busy, and one of its jobs appears to be sorting and strengthening memories formed during the day. Researchers call this process consolidation.

In many experiments, people who learn something and then sleep remember it better than people who stay awake for the same amount of time. Recordings of brain activity suggest why: during deep sleep, patterns of activity linked to recent learning are replayed, as if the brain were rehearsing. Sleep also seems to help the brain decide what to keep and what to let fade.

The practical point is that cutting sleep to study longer can backfire. A tired brain learns less efficiently the next day, and the material studied late at night may not be consolidated well. Spreading learning over several days, with sleep in between, tends to beat one long session. Rest is part of the learning, not a break from it.
g: Sleep helps memory because the brain uses it to sort and strengthen what was learned.
Studies show sleeping after learning improves memory because the brain replays recent learning during deep sleep.
Cutting sleep to study can backfire because tired brains learn less and late material is poorly consolidated.
k: Sleep helps consolidate memories formed during the day.
People who sleep after learning remember better; the brain seems to replay new learning.
Cutting sleep to study can backfire; spaced learning with sleep works better.

mc.s: What is the main message?
o: Sleep is an active part of learning and memory
Sleep is wasted time for students
Deep sleep only happens on weekends
mc.e: The passage argues sleep actively strengthens memory, ending with the line that rest is part of learning.

mc.s: You have an important presentation in three days. Based on the passage, which plan is best?
o: Practise a little each day and sleep normally
Stay up all night before the presentation
Practise only on the last morning
Skip sleep for two nights to free up time
mc.e: Spreading practice over days with sleep in between supports consolidation.

mc.s: What happens during deep sleep, according to recordings?
o: Activity linked to recent learning is replayed
New memories are deleted at random
mc.e: The second paragraph says patterns linked to recent learning are replayed.

o: the process of making memories stronger and more stable
v.d: In memory research, consolidation is how newly formed memories become stable and long-lasting.

o: have the opposite effect to the one intended
v.d: A plan that backfires produces the opposite of what was hoped.

passages.q: How can trade benefit a country even if it is better at making everything?
p: Imagine a lawyer who can also type faster than anyone in her office. Should she do her own typing? Probably not. Every hour she spends typing is an hour not spent on legal work, which earns far more. It makes sense for her to hire a typist, even one who types more slowly than she does.

Economists call this comparative advantage, an idea associated with the economist David Ricardo in the early nineteenth century. What matters is not who is absolutely best at a task, but who gives up the least to do it. The lawyer gives up a lot to type; the typist gives up little.

The same logic applies to countries. Even if one country can produce both cars and clothes more efficiently than another, both can gain if each specialises in what it gives up least to produce, and then they trade. Total output rises. Comparative advantage does not mean everyone wins from every trade deal, but it explains why trade so often creates value.
g: The lawyer should hire a typist because her time is worth more on legal work, even though she types faster.
This is comparative advantage, because what matters is who gives up least to do a task, not who is best at it.
Countries gain from specialising and trading because each produces what costs it least, raising total output.
k: The lawyer example: doing a task yourself has a cost in what you give up.
Comparative advantage is about who gives up least, not who is absolutely best.
Countries that specialise and trade can increase total output.

mc.s: What idea does the passage explain?
mc.e: The lawyer story introduces the concept, the second paragraph names it, the third applies it to countries.

mc.s: Why does the typist have a comparative advantage in typing?
o: The typist gives up less by spending time typing
The typist types faster than the lawyer
Typing is more valuable than law
mc.e: The passage says the typist is slower but gives up little, which is the definition of comparative advantage.

mc.s: Why does the author start with a lawyer rather than countries?
o: A familiar personal example makes the abstract idea easier to grasp
mc.e: The concrete case of one person’s time prepares the reader for the same logic at country level.

v.d: To specialise is to concentrate on a particular kind of work or product.

o: in a direct comparison of ability, without considering trade-offs
v.d: Here “absolutely best” means best in a straightforward head-to-head comparison, as opposed to comparatively.

passages.t: The wheat that fed a nation
passages.q: What changed Indian agriculture in the 1960s, and at what cost?
p: In the mid-1960s India faced serious food shortages after droughts, and relied heavily on imported grain. Within a decade, wheat production had risen sharply. The change became known as the Green Revolution.

It combined several things at once: new high-yielding varieties of wheat, developed partly from work by the plant scientist Norman Borlaug in Mexico, along with irrigation, chemical fertilisers and government support for farmers. Indian scientists, including M. S. Swaminathan, adapted these seeds to local conditions. Punjab and Haryana, with good irrigation, saw the biggest gains.

The results were mixed. Food security improved and famine became far less likely. But the gains were uneven between regions and crops, and intensive farming has strained groundwater and soil in the very states that benefited most. Historians now tend to describe the Green Revolution as both a success and a warning about the hidden costs of rapid gains.
g: India turned food shortages into rising wheat output in the 1960s because of what became the Green Revolution.
The gains came from a package of new seeds, irrigation, fertiliser and support, so irrigated states benefited most.
The legacy is mixed because food security improved but gains were uneven and the environment was strained.
k: India moved from food shortages to rising wheat production in about a decade.
High-yield seeds plus irrigation, fertiliser and support drove the change, especially in Punjab and Haryana.
It improved food security but brought uneven gains and environmental strain.

mc.s: What is the author’s overall view of the Green Revolution?
o: It was a real success with significant hidden costs
It solved all of India’s farming problems
mc.e: The final paragraph calls it both a success and a warning.

mc.s: Why did Punjab and Haryana gain most?
o: They had the irrigation the new seeds needed
mc.e: The passage links the biggest gains to good irrigation, part of the package that made the seeds work.

mc.s: Which problem is mentioned as a later cost?
mc.e: The third paragraph mentions strain on groundwater and soil.

o: producing a large amount of crop
v.d: High-yielding crops produce more grain per area of land.
Uneven gains are ones that some places or groups received far more of than others.

passages.q: What actually holds an aeroplane up?
p: A common explanation of flight says that air over the curved top of a wing must travel farther and so goes faster to “meet up” with air underneath. The first part is roughly right: air over the top does move faster. But the reason given is wrong. Nothing requires the two streams to meet again, and in fact the air over the top arrives well before the air underneath.

A better way to think about lift is that the wing turns the air. A wing is shaped and tilted so that it pushes the passing air downward. By Newton’s third law, if the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up. At the same time, the pressure above the wing drops and the pressure below rises, which is the same effect described in terms of pressure.

So the pressure explanation and the downwash explanation are not rivals. They describe one event from two angles. Pilots increase lift by raising the nose slightly or by extending flaps, both of which make the wing turn more air downward, especially at the low speeds of take-off and landing.
g: The “air must meet up” story of flight is wrong because the streams do not need to rejoin and the top air arrives first.
Wings make lift by pushing air downward, because the air pushes back up, which also shows up as a pressure difference.
Pressure and downwash are the same explanation from two angles, so pilots get more lift by making the wing turn more air.
k: The popular “equal transit” explanation of lift is wrong.
Wings push air downward, and the air pushes the wing up; this also appears as lower pressure above.
Pressure and downwash describe the same thing; flaps and angle increase lift.

mc.s: What is the main purpose of the passage?
o: To correct a common explanation of flight and offer a better one
To explain how jet engines work
To argue that flying is unsafe
To describe the history of flaps
mc.e: It opens by showing what is wrong with a popular explanation, then gives the better one.

mc.s: Why do pilots extend flaps when landing?
o: At low speed the wing needs to turn more air down to keep enough lift
Flaps reduce the weight of the plane
Flaps stop air reaching the top of the wing
mc.e: The final paragraph says flaps increase lift, which is especially needed at the low speeds of landing.

mc.s: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It concludes that the two explanations in paragraph two describe the same thing
mc.e: It draws the conclusion that pressure and downwash are not rivals but one event.

v.d: Rivals are competitors. Saying the explanations are not rivals means they do not compete; both are true.
Tilted means leaning or angled rather than flat.

passages.q: Why does the first number mentioned in a negotiation matter so much?
p: Ask people whether the tallest redwood tree is more or less than 1,200 feet tall, then ask them to guess its height. Their guesses will be far higher than those of people first asked about 180 feet. The first number acts like an anchor, and later judgements drift towards it.

Anchoring is one of the most reliably reproduced findings in psychology. It works even when people know the anchor is random, and even among experts. In one well-known study, experienced estate agents valuing a house were influenced by the listing price they were shown, while insisting they were not.

In negotiations, this means the first offer often shapes the final deal. Making the first offer can be an advantage when you know the value well, because it sets the anchor. When you do not, it can be safer to let the other side go first and then deliberately re-anchor with your own well-reasoned figure, rather than adjusting a little from theirs.
g: A first number acts as an anchor because later estimates drift towards it, as the redwood example shows.
Anchoring is robust because it affects people even when the anchor is random and even experts.
First offers shape deals, so make the first offer when you know the value, otherwise re-anchor with your own reasoned figure.
k: A first number becomes an anchor that pulls later estimates towards it.
Anchoring is robust: it affects experts and works even with random numbers.
In negotiation, set the anchor if you know the value; otherwise re-anchor deliberately.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How first numbers anchor judgements and what that means for negotiating
Why redwood trees are so tall
mc.e: It defines anchoring, shows it is robust, then applies it to negotiation.

mc.s: Why does the estate agent study matter to the argument?
o: It shows even experienced professionals are affected
It shows anchors only work on beginners
It shows people always notice anchors
mc.e: It supports the claim that anchoring works among experts, who denied being influenced.

mc.s: A supplier opens with a price you think is far too high, and you are unsure of the true value. What does the passage suggest?
o: Make your own well-reasoned counter-figure rather than nudging down from theirs
Offer a few per cent below their figure
mc.e: The passage recommends deliberately re-anchoring with your own reasoned figure.

o: found again when the experiment was repeated
v.d: A reproduced finding is one that other researchers got again when they repeated the study.
Deliberately means intentionally and with thought.

passages.t: A rehearsal for the immune system
passages.q: How does a vaccine prepare the body without causing the disease?
p: The immune system learns from experience. The first time it meets a particular germ, it takes days to recognise the invader and build a targeted response. During that delay, the person may become seriously ill. The second time, the response is much faster, because the body has kept a memory of the germ.

A vaccine gives the immune system that first experience safely. It shows the body a harmless version or piece of the germ, such as an inactivated virus or a single protein from its surface. The immune system responds as if it had met the real thing and stores memory cells that recognise it.

If the real germ arrives later, those memory cells can launch a rapid defence, often stopping the infection or making it much milder. Some vaccines need booster doses because memory fades over time or the germ changes. When enough people in a community are immune, a germ also struggles to spread, which protects people who cannot be vaccinated.
g: The immune system responds slowly the first time and fast the second, because it keeps a memory of the germ.
A vaccine provides that first encounter safely because it shows the body a harmless piece of the germ.
Later, memory cells allow a quick defence, so infections are stopped or milder, and community immunity protects others.
k: The immune system responds faster the second time it meets a germ.
Vaccines give a safe first encounter using a harmless version or piece of the germ.
Memory cells then defend quickly; boosters and community immunity extend protection.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: How vaccines use immune memory to protect people
mc.e: It sets up immune memory, then shows how vaccines create it safely and what follows.

mc.s: Why might a booster dose be needed?
o: Memory fades or the germ changes over time
The first dose was always faulty
mc.e: The third paragraph gives fading memory and changing germs as reasons.

mc.s: How does community immunity help people who cannot be vaccinated?
o: The germ struggles to spread when enough people are immune
They receive memory cells from others
They become immune by being near vaccinated people
mc.e: The passage says the germ struggles to spread, which protects those who cannot be vaccinated.

v.d: An inactivated virus has been treated so it cannot cause infection but can still be recognised by the immune system.
Rapid means happening quickly.

passages.t: The maths of a coffee shop
passages.q: Why can a busy coffee shop still struggle to make money?
p: A cup of coffee might sell for three pounds while the coffee, milk and cup cost well under a pound. That looks like an excellent business. But those ingredient costs are only a small part of the picture. Rent, staff wages, energy and equipment must all be paid whether the shop sells ten cups or a thousand.

These are fixed costs, and they explain why location and volume matter so much. A shop on a busy street pays high rent but may sell enough cups to cover it many times over. A cheaper side-street shop may never reach the number of sales needed just to break even. Each extra cup sold after that point is where the profit lies.

This is why coffee chains care about the morning rush, add food with higher margins, and design counters to serve people quickly. Speed is not just about customer satisfaction. In a business with high fixed costs, every extra customer served in a busy hour goes almost straight to profit.
g: Coffee looks very profitable per cup, but fixed costs like rent and wages are the bigger part of the picture.
Fixed costs make location and volume crucial because a shop must sell enough to break even before it profits.
Chains focus on speed and extra sales because, with high fixed costs, extra customers go almost straight to profit.
k: Ingredient costs per cup are small compared with fixed costs like rent and wages.
A shop must sell enough to break even; profit comes from sales beyond that point.
Speed and extra sales matter because extra customers add almost pure profit.

mc.s: What is the passage’s main point?
o: Fixed costs, not ingredients, decide whether a coffee shop profits
Side streets are better places for shops
mc.e: It contrasts the low cost per cup with high fixed costs and shows why volume matters.

mc.s: Why might adding pastries help a coffee shop’s profits?
o: They raise revenue from customers already paying for the fixed costs
Pastries are cheaper than coffee to sell
mc.e: The passage says food has higher margins and extra sales go towards profit once fixed costs are covered.

mc.s: What is the role of the second paragraph?
o: It explains why fixed costs make location and volume important
It describes how coffee is roasted
It argues against chain coffee shops
mc.e: It names fixed costs and draws out their consequence for location and break-even.

o: earn just enough to cover costs, with no profit or loss
v.d: To break even is to make exactly enough money to cover costs.

o: the profit left from each sale after its costs
v.d: In business, margin is the share of a sale’s price left after its direct costs.

passages.q: Why is the daytime sky blue rather than white?
p: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour has a different wavelength. Red light has the longest wavelength of the visible colours, and blue and violet the shortest.

When sunlight passes through the atmosphere, it meets countless gas molecules that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These molecules scatter short wavelengths far more strongly than long ones, an effect named after the physicist Lord Rayleigh. Blue light is scattered in all directions across the sky, so wherever we look, blue light reaches our eyes.

Violet is scattered even more, so why is the sky not violet? Partly because sunlight contains less violet, partly because some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and partly because our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset, light travels through much more air to reach us. Most of the blue is scattered away before it arrives, leaving the reds and oranges.
g: White sunlight is made of colours with different wavelengths, from long red to short blue and violet.
The sky is blue because small gas molecules scatter short blue wavelengths across the sky much more than red.
The sky is not violet because of less violet light, absorption and our eyes, and sunsets are red because blue is scattered away.
k: Sunlight is a mix of colours with different wavelengths.
Air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths far more, filling the sky with blue.
Violet is limited by sunlight, absorption and our eyes; sunsets are red because blue is scattered away.

mc.s: What does the passage mainly explain?
o: Why scattering of sunlight makes the sky blue and sunsets red
mc.e: The passage builds from light’s colours to scattering, then handles violet and sunsets.

mc.s: Why does a sunset look red?
o: Light passes through more air, so much of the blue is scattered away
The sun changes colour in the evening
Red light is scattered more than blue
mc.e: The final paragraph says longer paths scatter away blue, leaving reds and oranges.

mc.s: Why does the author raise the question about violet?
o: To handle an obvious objection to the explanation
To change the topic to rainbows
To show the explanation is wrong
mc.e: Violet is scattered even more, so a careful reader would ask why the sky is not violet; the author answers it.

v.d: To scatter light is to bounce it off in many directions.

o: quick to detect or respond to
v.d: Our eyes are less sensitive to violet means they respond to it less strongly.

passages.t: The rains that run an economy
passages.q: Why does the Indian monsoon matter so much beyond the weather?
p: Each summer, as the land of South Asia heats up faster than the surrounding ocean, moist winds blow in from the sea. They bring the southwest monsoon, which delivers most of India’s annual rainfall in roughly four months, from about June to September.

Because so much rain arrives in one season, its timing and amount ripple through the economy. A large share of Indian farmland depends on rain rather than irrigation. A weak monsoon can cut crop output, raise food prices and reduce rural incomes, which in turn means people buy fewer tractors, motorbikes and consumer goods.

That is why the India Meteorological Department’s monsoon forecast is watched by farmers, economists and investors alike. Reservoirs, hydroelectric power and groundwater also depend on it. Expanding irrigation and water storage has reduced the country’s exposure, but the monsoon remains one of the biggest single influences on how the year goes.
g: The monsoon comes because land heats faster than the sea, drawing in moist winds that bring most of the year’s rain.
The monsoon affects the whole economy because rain-fed farming links rainfall to food prices, incomes and spending.
Forecasts are closely watched because water and power depend on the monsoon, though irrigation has reduced the risk.
k: The monsoon brings most of India’s rain in about four summer months.
Much farming is rain-fed, so a weak monsoon hurts output, prices, incomes and spending.
The forecast is widely watched; irrigation and storage reduce but do not remove the dependence.

mc.s: What is the central idea?
o: The monsoon’s rainfall has effects far beyond farming, across the economy
India has the wettest climate in the world
Irrigation has made the monsoon irrelevant
mc.e: The passage shows how one season of rain ripples through farming, prices, spending and power.

mc.s: Why would a motorbike maker worry about a weak monsoon?
o: Lower rural incomes mean fewer purchases
mc.e: The second paragraph links weak rains to lower rural incomes and fewer purchases of goods like motorbikes.

mc.s: What has reduced India’s exposure to the monsoon?
mc.e: The final paragraph mentions expanding irrigation and storage.

o: spread outward in a series of effects
v.d: Effects that ripple through something spread outward, step by step, like rings on water.

o: the degree to which something is affected by a risk
v.d: Exposure to a risk is how much you are vulnerable to it.

passages.q: Why does money grow faster the longer it is left alone?
p: Suppose you invest one thousand pounds at seven per cent a year. After the first year you have seventy pounds of interest. If you leave it invested, the second year’s interest is calculated on one thousand and seventy pounds, not one thousand. You now earn interest on your interest. This is compounding.

In the early years the effect looks small. But it accelerates. At seven per cent, money roughly doubles in about ten years, doubles again in the next ten, and again in the ten after that. After thirty years, the original thousand would be worth around eight thousand, and most of that growth comes in the final decade.

This is why starting early matters so much, and why patience is such a powerful financial habit. It also works in reverse. Debts that charge interest on unpaid interest, such as credit card balances, can grow far faster than people expect. The same mathematics that rewards the saver punishes the borrower who waits.
g: Compounding means you earn interest on previous interest, because each year’s interest is added to the total.
Compounding accelerates because money keeps doubling, so most growth comes late.
Starting early pays off, but compounding also makes unpaid debts grow fast because it works in reverse.

Growth accelerates: at 7% money roughly doubles every ten years, with most gains late.
Starting early helps savers, and the same maths makes unpaid debt grow quickly.

Seven per cent is the best interest rate

Choosing a seven per cent investment

passages.q: Why was the printing press such a turning point?
p: Before the mid-fifteenth century, books in Europe were mostly copied by hand. A single book could take months, and books were rare and costly. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz developed a printing system that combined movable metal type, a suitable oil-based ink and an adapted press.

Each letter was cast as a separate piece of metal that could be arranged, inked, printed and then reused. A printing shop could produce hundreds of copies of a page far faster than any scribe. Within a few decades, presses had spread to hundreds of European towns and millions of books were in circulation.

Cheaper books changed more than reading. Ideas could spread quickly and in identical form, so scholars in different cities could work from the same text and correct it. Historians link printing to the spread of the Reformation and the growth of science. Printing had existed earlier in East Asia, but in Europe this particular combination changed how knowledge moved.
g: Hand-copied books were slow and expensive until Gutenberg combined movable type, ink and a press around 1450.
Printing spread fast because reusable metal letters let shops make many copies far more quickly than scribes.
Cheap identical books mattered because ideas could spread and be checked widely, linked to the Reformation and science.
k: Before printing, books were hand-copied, rare and expensive.
Gutenberg’s reusable movable type made copies fast; presses spread widely within decades.
Cheap, identical texts sped the spread of ideas, linked to the Reformation and science.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How Gutenberg’s press made books cheap and changed how ideas spread
mc.e: It covers the problem, the invention and its wider effects on knowledge.

mc.s: Why did identical copies matter for scholars?
o: They could compare and correct the same text from different cities
They could sell books for more
Identical books were easier to carry
mc.e: The third paragraph says scholars could work from the same text and correct it.

mc.s: What does the passage say about printing in East Asia?
mc.e: The last sentence notes printing existed earlier in East Asia.

o: being passed around and used by many people
v.d: Books in circulation are being sold, shared and read.

passages.q: Why are habits so hard to break by willpower alone?
p: A large share of what people do each day is done out of habit: the same route to work, the same coffee order, reaching for a phone when bored. Psychologists describe a habit as a behaviour that has become linked to a situation, so that the situation itself triggers the behaviour with little conscious thought.

This is why habits are tied so strongly to cues such as places, times and preceding actions. Studies of people who moved house or changed jobs suggest that a change of context can make it easier to change behaviour, because the old cues have disappeared. Willpower alone struggles against a behaviour that the environment keeps prompting.

The practical lesson is to work with cues rather than against them. To build a habit, attach it to a stable cue: stretch after brushing your teeth, read after dinner. To break one, remove or avoid the cue where possible, such as keeping the phone in another room while working. Repetition in the same context is what slowly makes a new behaviour automatic.
g: Habits are behaviours linked to situations, so the situation triggers them almost without thought.
Willpower struggles because cues keep prompting the behaviour, which is why changing context helps.
Work with cues: attach new habits to stable cues and remove the cues for unwanted ones.
k: A habit is a behaviour triggered by a situation with little conscious thought.
Cues keep prompting habits, so changing context can help change behaviour.
Attach new habits to stable cues; remove cues to break old ones; repeat in the same context.

mc.s: What is the main argument?
o: Habits are driven by cues, so changing cues works better than willpower alone
Willpower is the key to all habits
Habits form in exactly seven days
Moving house is always good for you
mc.e: The passage explains habits as cue-driven and builds advice around managing cues.

mc.s: You want to stop checking email first thing in the morning. What fits the passage best?
o: Leave your phone outside the bedroom overnight
Check email twice as often for a week
mc.e: Removing the cue, the phone by the bed, works with the habit mechanism.

mc.s: Why might starting a new job be a good time to build a habit?
o: Old cues are gone, so new behaviours face less competition
People have more willpower in new jobs
New jobs have fewer cues of any kind
mc.e: The second paragraph links changes of context to easier behaviour change.

v.d: Preceding actions are ones that happen just before something else.
An automatic behaviour happens on its own, without deliberate decision.

passages.q: How does a central bank try to keep prices stable?
p: Most countries have a central bank, such as the Bank of England or the Reserve Bank of India. One of its main jobs is to keep inflation, the general rise in prices, low and stable. In the UK, the government has set the Bank a target of two per cent inflation a year.

The main tool is the interest rate the central bank charges or pays to other banks. When it raises that rate, borrowing becomes more expensive across the economy and saving becomes more attractive. People and businesses tend to spend less, which eases pressure on prices. When it cuts the rate, the opposite happens, encouraging spending.

The difficulty is timing. Changes in interest rates take many months, often a year or more, to have their full effect. So central banks must act on forecasts of where inflation is heading, not where it is today. Raise rates too slowly and inflation can become entrenched; raise them too far and the economy may slow more than intended.
g: A central bank’s key job is keeping inflation low and stable, for example at a two per cent target in the UK.
It mainly uses interest rates, because higher rates cut spending and ease prices while lower rates do the opposite.
Timing is hard because rate changes act with long delays, so banks must act on forecasts and risk going too slow or too far.
k: Central banks aim to keep inflation low and stable, e.g. a 2% target.
Raising interest rates reduces spending and price pressure; cutting them encourages spending.
Effects take a year or more, so decisions rely on forecasts and risk over- or under-shooting.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: How central banks use interest rates to manage inflation, and why it is difficult
How to open a bank account
mc.e: It covers the goal, the tool and the timing problem.

mc.s: Why must central banks act on forecasts?
o: Rate changes take a long time to work, so today’s decision affects future inflation
mc.e: The third paragraph says effects take many months, often over a year.

mc.s: What happens when a central bank raises interest rates?
o: Borrowing becomes more expensive and spending tends to fall
mc.e: The second paragraph describes higher borrowing costs and reduced spending.

o: firmly established and hard to remove
v.d: Something entrenched is deeply fixed in place and difficult to change.
To ease pressure is to make it less.

passages.q: How does a cat turn over in mid-air without anything to push against?
p: Drop a cat upside down from a safe height and it will usually land on its feet. This puzzled scientists for a long time, because physics says a body cannot start spinning in mid-air without pushing against something. How can the cat turn over with nothing to push on?

High-speed photographs, first taken in the 1890s, revealed the trick. The cat bends in the middle and rotates its front and back halves in different ways. It tucks its front legs in to turn the front half quickly, while extending its back legs so the back half turns only a little the other way. Then it reverses the move. The two halves twist against each other, and overall the cat ends up the right way up without breaking any law of physics.

This righting reflex develops in kittens within their first few months. It does not make cats invincible. They need enough height to complete the turn, and a fall from a great height can still cause serious injury.
g: Cats land on their feet, which puzzled scientists because physics says you cannot start spinning without something to push on.
Photographs showed cats twist their two halves against each other, so they turn over without breaking physics.
The reflex develops early but has limits, because cats need enough height and can still be hurt.
k: Cats right themselves in mid-air, which seemed to defy physics.
They bend and rotate front and back halves in opposite ways, using legs to control each half.
The reflex appears in kittens but cats still need height and can be injured.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How cats turn over in mid-air without breaking physics
mc.e: It sets up the puzzle, explains the solution, then adds limits.

mc.s: Why does the cat tuck in its front legs?
o: Tucking in makes that half easier to turn quickly
To protect its face from the ground
mc.e: The passage says tucking the front legs turns the front half quickly, while extended back legs turn less.

mc.s: How does the second paragraph relate to the first?
o: It answers the puzzle the first paragraph raises
It gives a second, unrelated puzzle
It argues against the first paragraph
mc.e: The first paragraph ends with a question; the second answers it.

o: an automatic response the body makes without thinking
v.d: A reflex is an automatic, unlearned response, such as blinking.
Invincible means unable to be beaten or harmed.

passages.q: How useful is the idea that 20 per cent of causes produce 80 per cent of results?
p: The Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed around 1900 that a small share of people owned most of the land in Italy. Later writers generalised his observation into the “80/20 rule”: a minority of causes often produces a majority of effects. A few customers bring most of the revenue; a few bugs cause most of the crashes.

The rule is useful as a prompt to look for imbalance. If a small number of products, clients or tasks drive most of the value, attention can be focused there. Many businesses that check find something like this pattern, and it can change how they spend their time and money.

But 80 and 20 are not laws of nature. The real split might be 60/40 or 95/5, and in some situations effects are spread fairly evenly. The two numbers also need not add up to a hundred. The sensible use of the rule is to measure the actual distribution rather than assume it, and then act on what the data shows.
g: The 80/20 rule came from Pareto’s observation and says a few causes often produce most effects.
It is useful because it prompts you to find the few things that drive most value and focus on them.
The numbers are not fixed laws, so you should measure the real split before acting.
k: Pareto’s observation became the 80/20 rule: a minority of causes often drives most effects.
It is useful as a prompt to find and focus on the few drivers of value.
The split varies, so measure the real distribution instead of assuming 80/20.

mc.s: What is the author’s view of the 80/20 rule?
o: Useful as a prompt, but the actual split must be measured
mc.e: The second paragraph praises its usefulness; the third warns against treating the numbers as fixed.

mc.s: A manager assumes 20% of clients bring 80% of revenue without checking. What would the author say?
o: Check the actual data before acting
Drop the other 80% of clients immediately
mc.e: The final paragraph urges measuring the actual distribution rather than assuming it.

mc.s: What did Pareto originally observe?
o: A small share of people owned most land in Italy
Most crashes come from a few bugs
mc.e: The first paragraph describes his observation about land ownership.

o: turned into a broad rule from a specific case
v.d: To generalise is to take something observed in one case and apply it widely.

o: the way something is spread across a group
v.d: A distribution describes how amounts are spread, for example how revenue is spread across customers.

passages.t: Why most plastic is not recycled
passages.q: Why does so little plastic actually get recycled?
p: Many people assume that plastic placed in a recycling bin becomes new plastic. Much of it does not. Estimates suggest that only a small fraction of all plastic ever produced worldwide has been recycled, while most has been landfilled, burned or leaked into the environment.

Part of the reason is that “plastic” is not one material. There are many types with different chemistry, and they generally cannot be melted down together. Sorting them is costly, and food residue or mixed materials, such as a plastic film glued to paper, can make items impossible to recycle. Each time plastic is mechanically recycled, its quality also tends to fall.

Economics adds to the problem. New plastic made from oil and gas is often cheaper than recycled plastic, especially when oil prices are low. For this reason many experts argue that reducing and reusing plastic matters more than recycling it, and that products should be designed from the start using fewer, easier-to-recycle materials.
g: Most plastic is not recycled, despite what people assume, because most ends up landfilled, burned or leaked.
Recycling is hard because plastics are many different materials that are costly to sort, often contaminated, and degrade.
New plastic is often cheaper, so experts stress reducing, reusing and designing for recycling.
k: Only a small fraction of plastic ever made has been recycled.
Plastics are many different materials; sorting, contamination and quality loss make recycling hard.
Virgin plastic is often cheaper, so reducing, reusing and better design matter more.

mc.s: What is the passage’s main point?
o: Technical and economic barriers mean most plastic is not recycled
Burning plastic is the best option
mc.e: It corrects an assumption and then gives technical and economic reasons.

mc.s: Why might a crisp packet made of plastic layered with foil be hard to recycle?
o: It mixes materials that cannot easily be separated
It is too small to see
It is made only of paper
It has no plastic in it
mc.e: The second paragraph says mixed materials can make items impossible to recycle.

mc.s: Why does the economics of recycling sometimes fail?
o: New plastic from oil and gas is often cheaper
mc.e: The third paragraph says virgin plastic is often cheaper, especially when oil is cheap.

v.d: Residue is what remains after something has been used or removed, such as traces of food.

o: by physical processes such as shredding and melting
v.d: Mechanical recycling uses physical processes like grinding and melting rather than chemical breakdown.

passages.q: Why do people keep investing in things that are clearly failing?
p: You have paid for a concert ticket, but on the night you feel ill and the weather is awful. Many people go anyway, reasoning that they have already paid. Yet the money is gone whether they go or not. The only real question is whether the evening will be better at the concert or at home.

Costs that have already been paid and cannot be recovered are called sunk costs. Rational decisions should depend only on future costs and benefits. But people find it painful to admit that past spending was wasted, so they keep going to justify it. The tendency is known as the sunk cost fallacy.

In organisations, the effect can be expensive. Projects that are clearly failing receive more money because so much has already been spent, and leaders who started them may feel their reputation is at stake. A useful question is: if we were starting from scratch today, knowing what we now know, would we choose this? If not, the past spending is not a reason to continue.
g: Going to the concert because you paid is a mistake because the money is gone either way; only the evening ahead matters.
This is the sunk cost fallacy, because people keep going to avoid admitting past spending was wasted.
Organisations waste money this way, so ask whether you would choose the project if starting fresh today.
k: Already-spent money should not drive decisions; only future costs and benefits matter.
Continuing to justify past spending is the sunk cost fallacy.
Ask: would we choose this from scratch today? If not, stop.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: The sunk cost fallacy and how to avoid it
mc.e: The concert example introduces it, the second paragraph names it, the third applies it.

mc.s: A team has spent £2m on software that clearly will not work. Using the passage, what is the right question?
o: Would we start this project today, knowing what we know?
How can we avoid wasting the £2m?
How much more would it take to finish?
mc.e: The passage recommends judging from scratch, setting past spending aside.

mc.s: Why might a leader resist cancelling a failing project they started?
o: They feel their reputation is tied to it
mc.e: The third paragraph says leaders may feel their reputation is at stake.

v.d: A fallacy is an error in reasoning that can seem convincing.

v.d: To justify something is to give reasons that make it seem right.

passages.q: How does para sport make competition fair between athletes with different impairments?
p: In para sport, athletes have a wide range of impairments, from limb loss to visual impairment to conditions that affect muscle control. If everyone raced together, the result might depend more on the type of impairment than on training and talent. Classification is the system designed to prevent this.

Athletes are assessed by trained classifiers and placed into sport classes. Each class groups athletes whose impairments affect performance in that sport to a similar degree. In swimming, for example, classes are labelled with a letter and a number; a lower number generally indicates a greater impact on performance.

Classification aims to ensure that winning depends on skill, fitness and determination. It is not perfect. Impairments vary, assessments can be disputed, and the rules are reviewed as research improves. But without it, many athletes would have no fair chance to compete, and the sport would lose much of its meaning.
g: Para sport uses classification because otherwise results might depend on impairment type rather than ability.
Classifiers group athletes with similar impact on performance into sport classes, such as numbered swimming classes.
Classification aims to let skill decide results, and though imperfect it gives athletes a fair chance.
k: Classification stops results depending on impairment rather than training and talent.
Trained classifiers group athletes with similar impact into sport classes.
It aims to make skill decide results; it is imperfect and reviewed, but essential.

mc.s: What is the purpose of classification in para sport?
o: To make competition depend on ability rather than type of impairment
To reduce the number of athletes
mc.e: The passage says it is designed so winning depends on skill, fitness and determination.

mc.s: Why might the classification rules change over time?
o: Research improves understanding of how impairments affect performance
mc.e: The last paragraph says rules are reviewed as research improves.

mc.s: In swimming, what does a lower class number generally indicate?
mc.e: The second paragraph explains this.

v.d: An impairment is a reduction in a body function or structure, such as limb loss or low vision.

passages.t: How your phone knows where it is
passages.q: How does GPS work out your position?
p: The Global Positioning System relies on a constellation of around thirty satellites orbiting about 20,000 kilometres above the Earth. Each one carries extremely precise atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts a signal saying, in effect, “I am here, and this is the exact time.”

Your phone does not send anything to the satellites. It simply listens. Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, the tiny delay between when a signal was sent and when it arrived tells the phone how far away that satellite is. With distances to at least four satellites, the phone can calculate its position and correct for errors in its own, much less precise clock.

The timing has to be astonishingly accurate. An error of a millionth of a second would put you about 300 metres out. The system even corrects for effects predicted by Einstein’s theories of relativity, which make clocks on the satellites run at a slightly different rate from clocks on the ground. Without these corrections, positions would drift by kilometres each day.
g: GPS uses about thirty satellites with precise clocks that broadcast their position and the exact time.
Your phone listens and uses signal delays to measure distances to four satellites, so it can calculate its position.
Timing must be extremely precise, so the system even corrects for relativity to avoid large errors.
k: GPS satellites broadcast their location and precise time.
A phone measures signal delays from at least four satellites to calculate position.
Tiny timing errors matter, so GPS corrects for relativity.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: How GPS uses precise timing from satellites to find your position
How phones send signals to satellites
mc.e: It describes the satellites, how the phone calculates position, and why timing must be exact.

mc.s: Why does the phone need a fourth satellite?
o: To correct for errors in its own less precise clock
Because one satellite is always broken
mc.e: The second paragraph says four satellites let the phone correct its own clock errors.

mc.s: Does your phone send signals to GPS satellites?
mc.e: The passage says the phone does not send anything; it simply listens.

o: a group of objects arranged in space
v.d: Constellation usually means a group of stars; here it means a coordinated group of satellites.

o: move gradually away from where it should be
v.d: To drift is to move slowly and steadily off course.

passages.q: What makes dough rise and bread soft?
p: Yeast is a living, single-celled fungus. When it is mixed into dough with flour and water, it feeds on sugars, some of which are released from the flour’s starch. As it feeds, it produces carbon dioxide gas and small amounts of alcohol. This process is fermentation.

The gas alone would simply escape if the dough could not hold it. That is the job of gluten, a network of proteins that forms when wheat flour is mixed with water and kneaded. Kneading stretches and aligns the gluten into an elastic web that traps the gas in thousands of tiny bubbles, so the dough swells.

In the oven, the heat makes the gas expand further and evaporates the alcohol, before killing the yeast and setting the structure. The bubbles become the holes you see in a slice. This is why flours with less gluten-forming protein, such as rye, produce denser loaves, and why gluten-free bakers often add other ingredients to help hold the gas.
g: Dough rises because yeast feeds on sugars and produces carbon dioxide gas, a process called fermentation.
Gluten traps the gas because kneading builds an elastic protein web that holds it in bubbles.
Baking expands and sets the bubbles, so low-gluten flours make denser bread.
k: Yeast ferments sugars, producing carbon dioxide.
Kneaded gluten forms an elastic web that traps the gas.
Oven heat expands and sets the bubbles; less gluten means denser bread.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: How yeast and gluten work together to make bread rise
mc.e: It covers gas production, gas trapping and what happens in the oven.

mc.s: What would happen to dough that is barely kneaded?
o: It would trap less gas and rise less
mc.e: Kneading builds the gluten web that traps gas; less kneading means a weaker web.

mc.s: Why are rye loaves often denser?
o: Rye is baked at a lower temperature
mc.e: The final paragraph gives this reason.

o: able to stretch and return to shape
v.d: Elastic materials can stretch and then spring back.

o: arranges into lines or the same direction
v.d: To align is to arrange things in a straight line or the same direction.

passages.q: Is overuse of shared resources inevitable?
p: In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin described what he called the tragedy of the commons. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more cow, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone. So each keeps adding cows, and the pasture is ruined for all.

Hardin’s idea was influential and seemed to suggest only two solutions: turn the commons into private property, or let the government control it. Many fisheries, forests and grazing lands were managed on that assumption.

The political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged this. She studied communities around the world, from Swiss alpine pastures to irrigation systems in Nepal, that had managed shared resources well for generations. They succeeded through clear boundaries, rules shaped by users, monitoring and graduated penalties. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in economics, largely for showing that the tragedy is a risk, not an inevitable outcome.
g: Hardin’s tragedy of the commons says shared resources get overused because each user gains fully but shares the cost.
His idea led people to assume only privatisation or government control could work.
Ostrom showed communities can manage commons well with good rules, so the tragedy is a risk rather than a certainty.
k: The tragedy of the commons: individual gain and shared cost lead to overuse.
This led to an assumption that only privatisation or state control works.
Ostrom showed communities can manage commons with good rules; overuse is not inevitable.

mc.s: What is the main point of the passage?
o: Ostrom showed shared resources can be managed well, challenging Hardin’s pessimism
Hardin proved shared land always fails
mc.e: The passage sets up Hardin’s idea, its consequences, and then Ostrom’s challenge.

mc.s: Why does each herder add another cow in Hardin’s story?
o: They get the full gain but share the cost
They want to help the others
mc.e: The first paragraph explains the imbalance between private gain and shared cost.

mc.s: How is the passage organised?
o: An idea, its influence, and then a challenge to it
A story told in reverse order
mc.e: Paragraph one gives the idea, two its influence, three the challenge.

v.d: Graduated penalties start small and become larger for repeated or serious breaches.
Inevitable means bound to happen and impossible to avoid.

passages.q: Why are cities often warmer than the countryside around them?
p: On a still summer night, a city centre can be several degrees warmer than nearby fields. This is the urban heat island effect, and it has several causes that add up.

Dark surfaces such as roads and roofs absorb more sunlight than grass or trees, then release that heat slowly after dark. Buildings trap heat between them and block cooling winds. Cities also have fewer plants, which normally cool the air by releasing water through their leaves. And cars, air conditioners and industry add their own waste heat.

The effect matters because heatwaves are dangerous, especially for older people, and are becoming more common. Cities are responding with tree planting, green roofs, parks and lighter-coloured surfaces that reflect more sunlight. These measures do not stop heatwaves, but they can lower local temperatures and make the hottest days less harmful.
g: Cities can be several degrees warmer than fields, an effect called the urban heat island.
This happens because dark surfaces store heat, buildings trap it, there are fewer plants and machines add waste heat.
It matters because heatwaves harm people, so cities use trees, green roofs and lighter surfaces to cool down.
k: Cities are often warmer than surrounding areas: the urban heat island.
Causes: dark surfaces, trapped heat, fewer plants and waste heat.
Trees, green roofs and reflective surfaces can reduce the harm of heatwaves.

mc.s: What does the passage mainly describe?
o: The causes of urban heat islands and how cities respond
Why heatwaves are caused by cities
mc.e: It names the effect, gives causes, then responses.

mc.s: Why would replacing a car park with a park help?
o: Plants cool the air and absorb less heat than dark tarmac
Parks are cheaper than car parks
mc.e: The passage links plants to cooling and dark surfaces to stored heat.

mc.s: Why do dark surfaces matter at night?
o: They release stored heat slowly after dark
mc.e: The second paragraph says they absorb sunlight and release heat slowly after dark.

v.d: To absorb is to take something in, such as heat or light.

o: send back light or heat from a surface
v.d: A surface that reflects sunlight bounces it away instead of absorbing it. (It can also mean to think carefully, but not here.)
